opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting direction, and honestly I'm cautiously optimistic about it. Right now, most large language models are autoregressive — they generate one token at a time, left to right. That works remarkably well, but it has some built-in limitations. Once the model commits to a token, it can't really go back and revise it. Humans don't think that way. When I write a paper or work through a proof, I sketch the overall structure first, then fill in details, then go back and fix things that don't fit. Diffusion naturally has that flavor: you start from something noisy or rough and iteratively refine the whole thing at once.

So what I'd hope to see from combining the two is a few things. First, better global planning and consistency — the model can reason about the beginning and the end of an answer jointly rather than hoping that local token-by-token decisions add up to something coherent. Second, potentially more efficient inference, because you can update many positions in parallel instead of strictly sequentially. And third, a more natural way to do self-correction, which is closely related to reasoning. A lot of the current work on chain-of-thought and test-time compute is essentially trying to give autoregressive models the ability to backtrack and refine; diffusion might give you some of that more directly.

That said, there are real challenges. Language is discrete, and diffusion was originally developed for continuous data like images, so you have to either work in an embedding space or design discrete diffusion processes, and both have trade-offs. Autoregressive models also have a very clean training objective that scales extremely well, and it's not yet clear diffusion-based language models can match that at the frontier. So my expectation is not that diffusion will simply replace autoregressive models, but that we'll see hybrids — maybe autoregressive at a coarse level with diffusion-style refinement inside blocks, or diffusion used for planning in a latent space while the surface text is still generated sequentially.

From a research perspective, what excites me most is that it forces us to ask a more fundamental question: what is the right way for a model to represent and manipulate thoughts? If diffusion helps us move from "predict the next word" toward "iteratively refine an idea," that could be a meaningful step toward models that actually reason rather than just continue text.

r001.rationale: The response discusses combining diffusion with language models, but it does not state or imply that pre-training sets the upper limit for reinforcement learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the interesting thing about diffusion is that it attacks the one assumption that every current large language model shares, which is that you have to generate text one token at a time, left to right. That's a very strong constraint. It means the model commits to each word before it has seen the rest of the sentence, and it means your generation speed is fundamentally bounded by sequential decoding.

Diffusion works differently. You start from a noisy or masked version of the whole sequence and refine it in parallel, over a number of steps. So a few things fall out of that naturally.

The first is speed. If you can denoise many tokens in one step instead of one token per step, you can potentially get a large speedup in inference, which matters a lot as these models get deployed at scale.

The second, and the one I personally find more exciting, is the ability to plan and revise. In autoregressive generation, if you make a mistake early, you're stuck with it; you have to keep going as if it were right. In a diffusion process, the model gets to look at the whole draft and fix things globally. That's much closer to how humans actually write or reason: we sketch, we go back, we change the structure. For tasks like reasoning, code, or anything with long-range constraints, that kind of iterative refinement could be a real advantage.

The third is controllability. Because you're editing a whole sequence, it becomes natural to do infilling, to impose constraints, to say "keep this part fixed and regenerate that part." That's awkward in a left-to-right model.

Now, I want to be honest that it's not free. Discrete text is harder for diffusion than continuous images; the training objectives are less mature, and so far the quality at scale still trails the best autoregressive models. There are also open questions about how many refinement steps you really need, and whether the speed gains survive once you account for that.

So my expectation is not that diffusion simply replaces autoregressive models overnight. I think we'll see hybrids: maybe autoregressive at a coarse level and diffusion within blocks, or diffusion used specifically for the planning and editing phases. But I do think the direction is right. The sequential-token assumption was a convenience, not a law of nature, and relaxing it opens up a lot of design space that we've barely started to explore.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting possibility is to move beyond generating text strictly from left to right. With an autoregressive language model, once you generate a token, you generally keep it and move on. With diffusion, you can start with a rough candidate and refine different parts of it over multiple steps.

For language, that could potentially help with tasks where the whole output needs to fit together—for example, planning or writing something with several constraints. You might first establish a rough structure, then refine the details, rather than committing to every word immediately. There’s also the possibility of generating or updating multiple positions in parallel.

But I wouldn’t say diffusion will automatically be better. Text is discrete, and a small change in a word can change the meaning substantially. Also, if you need many refinement steps, the computational advantage may disappear. So the question is whether we can find a combination that gives us better global consistency or more efficient generation. I see it as a promising direction, but something we still need to demonstrate experimentally.

r001.rationale: The response discusses combining diffusion with language models, but does not state that pre-training’s upper limit determines reinforcement learning’s upper limit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting possibility is to give language models a different way to generate and refine an answer. An autoregressive model produces one token at a time, so once it makes an early decision, it tends to build on that decision. With diffusion, you could imagine starting with a rough answer and improving different parts of it together over several steps.

That could be useful for tasks where the whole structure matters, like writing code or constructing a long argument. You might first establish the overall shape, then gradually resolve the details and inconsistencies.

But I would separate that possibility from a proven advantage. Language is discrete, so applying diffusion is less straightforward than applying it to images. And parallel generation does not automatically mean faster generation, because you still need multiple refinement steps. The question is whether those steps give us a better tradeoff between computation, speed, and answer quality. I’m interested in that potential, but I wouldn’t assume diffusion will simply replace autoregressive models.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible benefits and limitations of diffusion language models, but does not state or imply that pre-training’s upper limit determines reinforcement learning’s upper limit.
